They don't recycle the air in planes. The cabin is pressurized, yes, but it's not airtight.

New cabin air is brought in from the bleed-air system, filtered and cooled, and then pumped into the cabin. Then, in order to maintain a constant pressure, air is also allowed to exit via outflow valves, usually located near the tail of the plane.

There is always fresh air coming in and old air going out, because otherwise the plane would have to carry oxygen tanks, which would impose a severe weight penalty, and be cost-prohibitive. There ARE oxygen tanks onboard, but those are for use by the flight crew in an emergency, and are only to be used until they can descend to an altitude where it's no longer neede (usually below 12,000 feet). The masks that drop in such an emergency don't have any oxygen tanks at all. They generate oxygen via a chemical process, and only last for about 20 minutes or so (again, only to keep you alive until at a safe altitude).

New cabin air is brought in from the bleed-air system, filtered and cooled, and then pumped into the cabin. Then, in order to maintain a constant pressure, air is also allowed to exit via outflow valves, usually located near the tail of the plane.

They don't recycle the air in planes.

This is false.

Modern airliners DO recycle the air, replacing it with fresh bleed air at a significantly reduced rate, in order to save costs. This has the following effects:

  • Oxygen levels drop well below normal. Down to nearly half of normal. As you correctly point out they don't carry oxygen to correct this.
  • CO2 levels rise well above normal. Typically over twice of normal, but sometimes as high as 10x or more. This is probably worse than the low oxygen.
  • CO levels rise as well, and other toxic fumes are introduced due to maintenance issues in the re-circulation system and from the engines.

As if this wasn't bad enough: While the cabin is pressurized, they make no attempt to maintain it anywhere near sea level air pressure. Instead, at cruise altitudes, you get the same cabin pressure as you would on a 6,000 to 8,500 ft mountain top, which is enough by itself to induce altitude sickness in those not adjusted to that. If only the air was as clean as on a mountain top.
